title: Find the derivatives and integrals of a range of functions including the trigonometric functions and apply these to problems

lessons.title: Derivatives of standard functions
lessons.html:
What a derivative means

The derivative f'(x) gives the instantaneous rate of change of a function, the gradient of the tangent at a point. In agri business it answers questions like "how fast is revenue changing as price changes?" or "how quickly is a dam's volume changing as the level rises?"

From first principles: f'(x) = lim (h→0) [f(x + h) − f(x)] / h.

Standard derivatives

f(x)f'(x)
xⁿn xⁿ⁻¹
eˣeˣ
ln x1/x
sin xcos x
cos x−sin x
tan xsec² x

Trigonometric derivatives assume x is in radians.

Rules

  • Sum and constant multiple: (af + bg)' = af' + bg'.
  • Product rule: (uv)' = u'v + uv'.
  • Quotient rule: (u/v)' = (u'v − uv') / v².
  • Chain rule: d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) · g'(x).

Worked examples

  1. y = 3x⁴ − 5x + 2 gives y' = 12x³ − 5.
  2. y = x² sin x gives y' = 2x sin x + x² cos x (product rule).
  3. y = sin(3x) gives y' = 3 cos(3x) (chain rule).
  4. y = e^(2x) cos x gives y' = 2e^(2x) cos x − e^(2x) sin x.
  5. y = cos²x = (cos x)² gives y' = 2 cos x · (−sin x) = −sin 2x.

Higher derivatives

The second derivative f''(x) measures how the rate of change itself changes. For f(x) = sin x, f'' = −sin x. This property, f'' = −f, is the signature of oscillation, which is why sine and cosine model repeating patterns.

lessons.title: Integrals of standard functions
lessons.html:
Antiderivatives and integrals

Integration reverses differentiation. If F'(x) = f(x), then ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C, where C is the constant of integration. The definite integral ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) gives the net accumulated quantity, for example total water flowing into a dam over a period when f is the flow rate.

Standard integrals

f(x)∫ f(x) dx
xⁿ (n ≠ −1)xⁿ⁺¹ / (n + 1) + C
1/xln |x| + C
eˣeˣ + C
sin x−cos x + C
cos xsin x + C
sec² xtan x + C

Linear substitution

For a linear inside function: ∫ cos(ax + b) dx = (1/a) sin(ax + b) + C. Example: ∫ sin(2x) dx = −½ cos(2x) + C.

Substitution

When the integrand contains a function and its derivative, let u = g(x). Example: ∫ 2x cos(x²) dx. Let u = x², du = 2x dx, so the integral becomes ∫ cos u du = sin(x²) + C.

Definite integral example

∫ from 0 to π of sin x dx = [−cos x] from 0 to π = (−cos π) − (−cos 0) = 1 + 1 = 2. The area under one arch of the sine curve is 2 square units.

Checking

Always differentiate your answer to check that you get back the original function. This catches sign errors, which are common with sine and cosine.

lessons.title: Applying calculus to problems
lessons.html:
Rates of change in context

Suppose seasonal demand for a product, in hundreds of units per month, is modelled by D(t) = 50 + 30 sin(πt/6), where t is months from the start of the year. Then D'(t) = 30 · (π/6) cos(πt/6) = 5π cos(πt/6). At t = 0, D' = 5π ≈ 15.7 hundred units per month: demand is rising fastest. At t = 3, cos(π/2) = 0, so demand has reached a peak. This helps a buyer time orders before the peak.

Optimisation

To find maximum or minimum values, set f'(x) = 0, solve, and test with the second derivative (f'' < 0 for a maximum, f'' > 0 for a minimum) or check endpoints on a closed interval.

Example: profit P(x) = −2x² + 240x − 3,000 rand, where x is units sold per week. P'(x) = −4x + 240 = 0 gives x = 60. P'' = −4 < 0, so x = 60 gives maximum profit P(60) = −7,200 + 14,400 − 3,000 = R4,200.

Accumulation

If the total demand over the first six months is wanted from the model above, integrate: ∫ from 0 to 6 of [50 + 30 sin(πt/6)] dt = [50t − (180/π) cos(πt/6)] from 0 to 6 = 300 − (180/π)(−1) + (180/π)(1) = 300 + 360/π ≈ 414.6 hundred units.

Problem-solving steps

  1. Define variables and units.
  2. Write the function from the information given.
  3. Differentiate or integrate as needed.
  4. Solve and check (second derivative, endpoints, units).
  5. Interpret the answer in the business or farming context.

Key points

  • The derivative of sin x is cos x; of cos x is −sin x (x in radians).
  • Use product, quotient and chain rules for combined functions.
  • Integration reverses differentiation; add C for indefinite integrals.
  • Set f'(x) = 0 and use f'' to classify turning points.
  • Definite integrals give accumulated totals.
